english: Whatever, therefore, was the substance of the Word that I designate a Person, I claim for it the name of Son; and while I recognize the Son, I assert His distinction as second to the Father.

english: Now the Spirit indeed is third from God and the Son; just as the fruit of the tree is third from the root, or as the stream out of the river is third from the fountain, or as the apex of the ray is third from the sun. Nothing, however, is alien from that original source whence it derives its own properties. In like manner the Trinity, flowing down from the Father through intertwined and connected steps, does not at all disturb the Monarchy, while it at the same time guards the state of the Economy.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3; text as on newadvent.org, revised by Kevin Knight)
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 603 (Scribner 1918 printing, PDF p. 617)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885; 1918 Scribner printing, archive.org antenicenefather03robe); Migne, Patrologia Latina vol. 2 (1844)
what_it_says: The Spirit is third from God and the Son, as fruit is third from root, stream third from fountain, and the ray-tip third from the sun; the Trinity is an ordered descent that does not disturb the Monarchy.
use: supports: the Spirit is a distinct third in the economy and is not separable from the Father; the image is used to show distinction and ordering without division.
limits: The brief locates "tertius est spiritus a Deo et Filio" in ch. 25; it is in ch. 8 (Migne col. 0164A; ANF p. 603). Ch. 25 has no "tertius est spiritus". The image is an ordering (gradus), and "third" can be read as rank, which is what an Arian reader would press. Tertullian answers that the Monarchy is kept by unity of substance; the image alone does not show that.

In the same manner, the other passages also establish each one of several Persons in His special character — addressed as they in some cases are to the Father or to the Son respecting the Son, in other cases to the Son or to the Father concerning the Father, and again in other instances to the (Holy) Spirit.

limits: The argument rests on the grammatical persons of Scripture speech. A Praxean can reply that God speaks to himself in those texts; Tertullian answers that he has already set out the Son as a distinct Person, so this item proves distinction only when read with ch. 7 and 12.

english: In what sense, however, you ought to understand Him to be another, I have already explained, on the ground of Personality, not of Substance — in the way of distinction, not of division. But although I must everywhere hold one only substance in three coherent and inseparable (Persons), yet I am bound to acknowledge, from the necessity of the case, that He who issues a command is different from Him who executes it.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3; text as on newadvent.org, revised by Kevin Knight)
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 607 (Scribner 1918 printing, PDF p. 621)

what_it_says: Tertullian says "another" must be taken in the sense of person (persona), not substance, and of distinction, not division; he holds one substance in three coherent persons.
use: answer to objection: this is the explanatory sentence for the "alius" and "alium" texts of the work (ch. 9, 12, 18, 19), and it is the direct Trinitarian reply to the charge of "two Gods".
limits: Tertullian does not say homoousios and does not define "persona" in the later Nicene sense. The ANF "(Persons)" in brackets is the translator's gloss.

what_it_says: Tertullian argues that Isa. 45:5 ("there is none else beside me") does not deny the Son, because the Son is not another God and is not "other" than the Father.

limits: Hard passage. "caeterum alius a Patre Filius non est" can be read as denying any real distinction, which is the Praxean reading; Tertullian's point depends on the contrast with "alium Deum". english: Since they are unwilling to allow that the Son is a distinct Person, second from the Father, lest, being thus second, He should cause two Gods to be spoken of, we have shown above that Two are actually described in Scripture as God and Lord. And to prevent their being offended at this fact, we give a reason why they are not said to be two Gods and two Lords, but that they are two as Father and Son; and this not by severance of their substance, but from the dispensation wherein we declare the Son to be undivided and inseparable from the Father — distinct in degree, not in state.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3; text as on newadvent.org, revised by Kevin Knight)

what_it_says: If they refuse to count the Son as second from the Father for fear of two Gods, Tertullian replies that Scripture also calls two God and two Lord, and that the Son is distinct in degree, not in state, while one God.
use: answer to objection: the "two Gods" charge is answered by "not by separation of substance but by dispensation" and "degree not state". The sentence answers the claim that the Son is a second God.
limits: Hard passage. "gradu" (degree) and "secundum" (second) are the words an Arian or subordinationist reader presses; Tertullian's reply is that the separation is in dispensation, not substance. what_it_says: The Word became flesh not by transformation of His substance but by really clothing Himself in flesh; transformation would destroy what was before, and God is unchangeable.

english: If, however, it was only a tertium quid, some composite essence formed out of the Two substances, like the electrum (which we have mentioned), there would be no distinct proofs apparent of either nature. But by a transfer of functions, the Spirit would have done things to be done by the Flesh, and the Flesh such as are effected by the Spirit; or else such things as are suited neither to the Flesh nor to the Spirit, but confusedly of some third character. Nay more, on this supposition, either the Word underwent death, or the flesh did not die, if so be the Word was converted into flesh; because either the flesh was immortal, or the Word was mortal. Forasmuch, however, as the two substances acted distinctly, each in its own character, there necessarily accrued to them severally their own operations, and their own issues.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3; text as on newadvent.org, revised by Kevin Knight)
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 624 (Scribner 1918 printing, PDF p. 638)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885; 1918 Scribner printing, archive.org antenicenefather03robe); Migne, Patrologia Latina vol. 2 (1844)
what_it_says: If the Word and flesh formed a third mixed substance, like electrum, the distinct proofs of each nature would not appear; they do appear, so the union is not a mixture.
use: answer to objection: the argument against a third or mixed substance in Christ keeps the separate properties of divinity and humanity in one Person.
limits: The electrum image is Tertullian's own and is used against a mixture, not against subordination. It does not answer a direct question about the Son's rank.

ref: 29 (chapter; the division is the same in Migne PL 2 and ANF; neither has section numbers)
latin: Obmutescat, obmutescat ista blasphemia, sufficiat Christum Filium Dei mortuum dici; et hoc quia ita scriptum est. Nam et Apostolus, non sine onere pronuntians Christum mortuum, adjecit, secundum Scripturas;
latin_edition: Migne PL 2 (1844), as transcribed on la.wikisource.org (Adversus Praxeam); column numbers from the transcription; cross-checked for each passage against the archive.org Migne PL 2 OCR (patrologiaecur02mign_djvu.txt), which agrees apart from OCR noise. Not checked against the page image: the Migne PDF (104 MB) is over the 60 MB limit and was not downloaded. Migne columns inside the span: 0194A; last column marker before the span: 0193D. Latin word count: 28.
english: Silence! Silence on such blasphemy. Let us be content with saying that Christ died, the Son of the Father; and let this suffice, because the Scriptures have told us so much. For even the apostle, to his declaration — which he makes not without feeling the weight of it — that Christ died, immediately adds, according to the Scriptures,
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3; text as on newadvent.org, revised by Kevin Knight)
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 625 (Scribner 1918 printing, PDF p. 639)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885; 1918 Scribner printing, archive.org antenicenefather03robe); Migne, Patrologia Latina vol. 2 (1844)
what_it_says: Tertullian says that "the Father died" is blasphemy; it is enough to say that Christ, the Son of God, died, as Scripture says (1 Cor. 15:3).
use: answer to objection: the "Pater passus" slogan is rejected; the death is attributed to Christ in the flesh, the anointed nature.
limits: Tertullian says the Son died "qua caro" (in respect of flesh), which is his own reading of 1 Cor. 15:3 and is the point an opponent will press against him. The same chapter states that the Spirit suffered only in the Son (see T5-17).

ref: 29 (chapter; the division is the same in Migne PL 2 and ANF; neither has section numbers)
latin: Ergo nec compassus est Pater Filio; sic enim directam blasphemiam in Patrem veriti, diminui eam hoc modo sperant, concedentes jam Patrem et Filium duos esse; si Filius quidem patitur, Pater vero compatitur. Stulti et in hoc. Quid est enim compati, quam cum alio pati? Porro, si impassibilis Pater, utique et incompassibilis. Aut si compassibilis, utique passibilis. Nihil ei vel hoc timore tuo praestas. Times dicere passibilem, quem dicis compassibilem. Tam autem incompassibilis Pater est, quam impassibilis etiam Filius ex ea conditione qua Deus est.
latin_edition: Migne PL 2 (1844), as transcribed on la.wikisource.org (Adversus Praxeam); column numbers from the transcription; cross-checked for each passage against the archive.org Migne PL 2 OCR (patrologiaecur02mign_djvu.txt), which agrees apart from OCR noise. Not checked against the page image: the Migne PDF (104 MB) is over the 60 MB limit and was not downloaded. Migne columns inside the span: 0194C; last column marker before the span: 0194B. Latin word count: 84.
english: On this principle, too, the Father was not associated in suffering with the Son. The heretics, indeed, fearing to incur direct blasphemy against the Father, hope to diminish it by this expedient: they grant us so far that the Father and the Son are Two; adding that, since it is the Son indeed who suffers, the Father is only His fellow-sufferer. But how absurd are they even in this conceit! For what is the meaning of fellow-suffering, but the endurance of suffering along with another? Now if the Father is incapable of suffering, He. is incapable of suffering in company with another; otherwise, if He can suffer with another, He is of course capable of suffering. You, in fact, yield Him nothing by this subterfuge of your fears. You are afraid to say that He is capable of suffering whom you make to be capable of fellow-suffering. Then, again, the Father is as incapable of fellow-suffering as the Son even is of suffering under the conditions of His existence as God.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3; text as on newadvent.org, revised by Kevin Knight)
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 626 (Scribner 1918 printing, PDF p. 640)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885; 1918 Scribner printing, archive.org antenicenefather03robe); Migne, Patrologia Latina vol. 2 (1844)
what_it_says: The Father is impassible and incapable of "fellow-suffering" (compassio), so the Father did not suffer with the Son; the Son is impassible as God.
use: answer to objection: the claim that the Father is "fellow-sufferer" with the Son is refuted on its own terms; supports the impassibility of the Father.
limits: Tertullian's argument is about what can be attributed to the Father. It does not explain how the Son is impassible as God and passible as man; that is left to the later chapters.

ref: 29 (chapter; the division is the same in Migne PL 2 and ANF; neither has section numbers)
latin: Sed quomodo Filius passus est, si non compassus est et Pater? Separabatur a Filio, non a Deo. Nam et fluvius si aliqua turbulentia contaminatur, quanquam una substantia de fonte decurrat, nec secernatur a fonte, tamen fluvii injuria non pertinebit ad fontem. Et licet aqua fontis sit quae patiatur in fluvio; dum non in fonte patitur, sed in fluvio, non fons patitur, sed fluvius qui ex fonte est. Ita, et si spiritus Dei quid pati posset in Filio, quia tamen non in Patre pateretur, sed in Filio, Pater passus non videretur.
latin_edition: Migne PL 2 (1844), as transcribed on la.wikisource.org (Adversus Praxeam); column numbers from the transcription; cross-checked for each passage against the archive.org Migne PL 2 OCR (patrologiaecur02mign_djvu.txt), which agrees apart from OCR noise. Not checked against the page image: the Migne PDF (104 MB) is over the 60 MB limit and was not downloaded. Migne columns inside the span: 0194D; last column marker before the span: 0194C. Latin word count: 90.
english: Well, but how could the Son suffer, if the Father did not suffer with Him? My answer is, The Father is separate from the Son, though not from Him as God. For even if a river be soiled with mire and mud, although it flows from the fountain identical in nature with it, and is not separated from the fountain, yet the injury which affects the stream reaches not to the fountain; and although it is the water of the fountain which suffers down the stream, still, since it is not affected at the fountain, but only in the river, the fountain suffers nothing, but only the river which issues from the fountain. So likewise the Spirit of God, whatever suffering it might be capable of in the Son, yet, inasmuch as it could not suffer in the Father, the fountain of the Godhead, but only in the Son, it evidently could not have suffered, as the Father.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3; text as on newadvent.org, revised by Kevin Knight)
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 626 (Scribner 1918 printing, PDF p. 640)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885; 1918 Scribner printing, archive.org antenicenefather03robe); Migne, Patrologia Latina vol. 2 (1844)
what_it_says: The Son suffered and the Father did not suffer with Him: the Father is separate from the Son in his flesh but not as God; the river is hurt, not the fountain, so the Spirit of God suffered only in the Son.
use: answer to objection: the fountain/river image answers "Pater passus" (the Father suffered): suffering is in the Son, not in the Father as the source of the Godhead.
limits: The ANF rendering of "Pater passus non videretur" ("could not have suffered, as the Father") is looser than the Latin ("the Father would not seem to suffer"). The fountain/river image can also be read as the Son being a derived stream. "Pater passus" in the Praxean sense also appears in ch. 2 (outside my range and not paged here; Latin "Itaque post tempus Pater natus, et Pater passus", a summary of the Praxean view) and ch. 30 ("Pater passus non est").
